tracks.title: The file that deploys you
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 6 — deployments. A sub-lesson, under nexus. The file that deploys you. [curious] You've been burned by a config file before. It started as ten honest keys — a name, a port, a region. And a year later it was a Turing-complete pipeline with an exec key, secret interpolation, and a templating language nobody chose. The word declarative was on the box… the contents were a program you couldn't read. So when the parent lesson says — flip local to cloud and your prototype is the product — your reflex is right. That's a brochure line… until proven otherwise. This page sets a bar, and then clears it. A deployment description you can hold in your head. Inert by construction, not by promise. We'll read the parser, watch the validator refuse to let you lie to yourself, and bring the same engine up on a laptop and on a public host.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: First — the definition. A deployment is an org file of five properties the engine converges to. Engine place… tenancy… storage… database… and auth. And here's the twist — the place it runs is one of them. Inert by construction: read by a property scan… never executed. Two words carry the whole lesson. Converges — you describe the end state, and the tooling makes reality match. No steps, no order, idempotent. And never executed — the file is read by a hand-rolled scan of a properties drawer, not by the org engine that tangles and runs other workbooks. [curious] This is the one org file in the system that is pure config and nothing else. And that's a property you can verify… not a posture.

tracks.title: Five axes, one screen
tracks.text: Now — five axes, one screen. Picture the real local deployment, shipped in the kit, whole. One headline named local… then a properties drawer with seven lines. An ID. Engine place, set to local. Tenancy mode, single. Storage, local-fs. Database, sqlite. And auth, trusted. That's the entire file. Five of those are closed enums — the only axes that exist. Let me walk them as a table, in plain speech. First, engine place — local or cloud, and it's required. It decides between a microVM on your mac… or a provider recipe. Second, tenancy mode — single or multi, defaulting to single. Multi means tenants who need identity and isolation. Third, storage — local-fs or s3, defaulting to local-fs. Either the working directory is the store… or it's an S3-compatible bucket. Fourth, database — sqlite or postgres, defaulting to sqlite. One writer… or many. And fifth, auth — trusted, betterauth, clerk, or oidc, defaulting to trusted. No identity… or a real token issuer. Everything else is an open property — a plain string an axis reads when it needs one. There is nothing else. [curious] And here's why we can say inert and mean it. The reader is about twenty lines. It walks the file top to bottom, flips a switch on when it sees the properties marker and off at the end marker, and inside the drawer it matches each line against one regular expression — colon, key, colon, then the value, trimmed. A line that matches contributes a key and a value. A line that doesn't match… is silently ignored. That's the whole parser. No interpolation. No hooks. No template language. No branch where a string becomes code. Declarative here is a measurable property of a reader you could screenshot — not a marketing adjective.

tracks.title: The honesty engine
tracks.text: Next — the honesty engine. A linter checks syntax. Validate checks truth. It runs with zero deploy — read-only, no machine touched — and its job is to refuse configurations that would lie to you. Its error messages aren't style notes… they're distributed-systems tradeoffs encoded as refusals. Here are three, quoted exactly. First — multi-tenant on a sqlite database is rejected, with the message… multi on database sqlite serializes every tenant through one writer, set database to postgres. Second — multi-tenant with trusted auth is rejected, because trusted has no identity to isolate tenants by. Third — s3 storage with missing secrets is rejected… because s3 needs its key and secret in your deploy environment. Secrets, not the file. [curious] Read what those refusals know. Multi-tenant on one sqlite writer doesn't fail — it works, slowly, funneling every tenant through a single lock until the day it doesn't. Trusted auth has no token, no subject, no identity — so there is literally nothing to scope a tenant by. And s3 demands its credentials from the environment, by name, because secrets in the file is the original sin. Picture the full set of checks as a flow. The config goes in. First gate — are the five axes legal values? If not, invalid. If yes, second gate — are the combinations coherent? Multi plus sqlite falls out here. Multi plus trusted falls out here. If they're coherent, third gate — are the required secrets present in the environment? S3 without its key falls out. Postgres without its database URL falls out — the DSN is a secret. Real auth without an issuer falls out — a token needs an issuer. And only if everything passes does it reach the green node, and print the shape it understood — valid, local, single-tenant, storage local-fs, database sqlite. [excited] The validator is the part of the system that refuses to let you write a config that would quietly lie.

tracks.title: A cloud on your desk
tracks.text: A cloud on your desk. This is a depth rung — skippable — but it's where local stops being a simulator. Local place is not a mock. It's the same runtime image cloud uses, booted in a real Linux microVM on your mac. That microVM is the outer isolation boundary — wrapped around the wasm sandbox each workbook runs in. Watch the bring-up, command by command. First… you run deploy doctor, and it reports — created the case-sensitive APFS volume, prereqs OK now. Second… you run deploy apply, and it says — local runtime up, at one-two-seven-dot-oh-dot-oh-dot-one, port five-five-one-two-three, survives app quit. Third… you run deploy verify, and it says — runtime healthy, health check returned two hundred. Under that calm output are two real macOS war stories. The one-time prereq — krunvm's store needs a case-sensitive APFS volume, which doctor creates for you, no sudo, non-destructive. Then the create command, with flags that each exist for a reason — two CPUs, two thousand megabytes of memory… a workdir of slash-app, because krunvm won't inherit the image's working directory… a port map from a free host port to the guest's fixed four thousand… and two volumes, your data, and a disco directory where the discovery handshake lands. Now the first war story — the boot command. You'd expect bin workbooks start. But start runs a foreground console that needs a terminal, and under krunvm's terminal-less guest it blocks before the app ever boots. Silent. So instead the boot is an eval expression — boot the app, then sleep forever; and on failure, halt with code one so it surfaces in the logs. [curious] Picture the sequence as a story. You call doctor — the volume is ready. You call create and start, passing the desktop environment flags. krunvm boots the image with eval, no terminal needed, and parks. Inside, the runtime writes a file — runtime dot json — into the disco mount, carrying the port, the pid, and a token. Your session polls that mount for up to twenty seconds… finds the file… reads the port and the bearer token… and hits the health endpoint with that token. The runtime answers two hundred, body contains okay. That's the handshake. And the second war story — why the VM survives you closing the app. libkrun needs your graphical session; run under a background agent it exits with code seventy-eight. So the default is a detached spawn into your session, with the pid in a file — it survives the app quitting, and dies on logout. When you finally run down, both lifecycles are removed and the VM is deleted — but your data and the APFS volume are preserved. Your data outlives the machine.

tracks.title: Five hooks and a tempfile
tracks.text: Five hooks and a tempfile. Cloud isn't magic either. A provider is a directory — a bootstrap shell script. The place resolves to a backend… local resolves to the built-in machine, anything else resolves to that script. Adding a provider is dropping a directory; the core never changes. Each recipe fills the same five hooks, plus a lifecycle trio. Let me read them. First, ensure app — create the app if it's missing. Second, set secrets — stage credentials, out of band. Third, attach volume — a persistent disk for slash-data. Fourth, deploy image — run the OCI image. Fifth, public url — print the address. And then down, status, and logs. [curious] Picture the flow. Apply asks — what's the engine place? Local routes to the built-in machine, the krunvm microVM. Cloud resolves the provider's bootstrap script and runs the up action, which fires those five hooks in order, ending at public url, which prints the address. Fly is the one bundled recipe — and the comment at the top says so plainly. Fly is our preference, not a privileged target, just one recipe behind a provider-neutral spine. Here's the concrete part. On apply, the Fly recipe creates the app if missing, stages the secrets, creates a one-gigabyte volume if absent — then synthesizes a minimal fly config in a temp directory, deploys it, and deletes it. Picture that config. The app is named my-app. Primary region, sjc. The build section points image at the runtime image. The mounts section binds a volume named wbdata to slash-data. And the http service section sets internal port four thousand, forces https, and turns on auto-stop and auto-start with a minimum of zero machines running — that's scale-to-zero. The public address is my-app dot fly dot dev. And the env every provider forwards is the quiet keystone — web mode on, port four thousand, data at slash-data, and crucially, the registry pointed at slash-data slash registry dot db. The registry defaults to in-memory — pointing it at the volume is exactly what makes deployed workbooks survive a restart or a scale-to-zero, with litestream replicating that database. The punchline is how small the contract is. A Hetzner, Render, or AWS recipe is the same ninety lines with different commands — because the engine asks the host for only four things. Run my container. Attach a volume. Deliver my secrets. Expose a port.

tracks.title: The actual diff
tracks.text: The actual diff. Now the parent's claim, made literal. Moving from local to cloud is editing engine place — and then adding exactly the properties the validator forces you to add. Picture the diff. On the left, the local file. On the right, the cloud file. Engine place changes from local to cloud. Then additions appear — a provider, fly. An app name. Tenancy mode goes from single to multi. Storage goes from local-fs to s3, and that drags in three more lines — an endpoint, a bucket, a region. Database goes from sqlite to postgres. Auth goes from trusted to clerk, which drags in an issuer. And a region, iad. None of those additions are decoration — each one is the validator refusing a half-edit. Try to go multi while still on sqlite and trusted, with s3 but no credentials, and validate stops you cold, listing — multi on sqlite serializes every tenant through one writer, set postgres… and s3 needs its key and secret in your deploy environment. So you don't add postgres because a guide told you to. You add it because multi demanded it. [curious] And the same translation runs in both directions — it's one function that turns the five axes into the engine's environment. Picture that as a table, local versus cloud. The storage env comes from the file's storage axis — local one side, s3 the other. Tenancy comes from the file — single, then multi. Bucket and endpoint come from the file, not secret. But the s3 key and secret come from your deploy environment — forwarded, never echoed. The database URL, the same — forwarded from the environment. The auth issuer comes from the file, with the JWKS path derived. And the image — generated, the same both ways. [excited] That last row is the whole one-property claim in a single line. The image is identical on both sides. Same image, same env-assembly function, two delivery mechanisms. Beyond that, the diff is the deploy.

tracks.title: Names in the file, values nowhere near it
tracks.text: Names in the file, values nowhere near it. Another depth rung — but it's the discipline that lets the file stay inert and public. The doctrine is stated in the header users read first. Secrets are not in this file. Axes live in the drawer; credentials live in your deploy environment. You declare secrets by name in the file. You set values with a secrets-set command, stored mode six-hundred in a secrets file under the app directory. And you list them by name only — list never prints a value. Locally they're delivered as an env-file; in the cloud they're staged through the provider's set-secrets hook. Values never enter the deployment file or any image. And apply refuses to deploy with a declared secret unset — it tells you which one, and how to set it. [curious] Picture the path a secret's value takes, as a graph. The value starts in your environment or the secrets file. It flows into the recipe's memory. Then it's staged through fly secrets set. And it lands in the container's environment. Off to the side sits the deployment file — connected by a dotted line that reads, never touched. It names the key… and touches the value never. Two secrets earn special handling, because they are your engine's identity. On the first cloud apply, the kit generates a public bearer token — thirty-two random bytes — exactly once, and never rotates it. Rotating would four-oh-one every live client and break the tenant's stable identity. And a signing key — a thirty-two byte seed — is the engine's identity document. Set it once and your engine survives every redeploy. Skip it… and the identity regenerates on each deploy, and every prior signature stops verifying.

tracks.title: Converge, prove, tear down
tracks.text: Converge, prove, tear down. The verbs are built for agents as much as humans — every one non-interactive, idempotent, takes a json flag, and exits non-zero on failure. The arc is init, validate, apply, then status, verify, or logs, then down. Plus two shortcuts — a zero-config local bring-up, like docker run… and doctor, to check and self-heal prereqs. Let me give the table as plain speech. Init writes a starter deployment file from a template, and won't clobber an existing one without force. Validate checks truth and deploys nothing, reading the file and your environment. Apply converges reality to the file — and re-running it is a no-op. Verify proves the live runtime. Status reports presence and the endpoint. Down tears everything down but keeps your data. And doctor checks and self-heals prereqs. Two rows carry the weight. Verify doesn't trust the deploy log — it proves the live engine. Locally it reads the discovery file and hits the health endpoint with the discovery token, expecting two hundred with okay. In the cloud it asks the provider for its URL, then hits that health endpoint. And doctor doesn't just diagnose — if the APFS volume is missing it creates it, and reports the system is ready. [excited] The contract — non-zero exit on failure, json on request — is what lets a workflow run the whole arc unattended… and a human run it by hand… from the same surface.

tracks.title: Where the seam ends
tracks.text: Where the seam ends — the honest part. The macOS path carries real, un-pretty engineering. The terminal-less boot hack and the graphical-session requirement aren't elegance — they're scars. The detached VM dies on logout, and the start-on-login path that would survive conflicts with libkrun. The default lifecycle is the one that works, not the one that's tidy. The cloud side ships exactly one recipe — Fly. The seam is provider-neutral by design, and any host fits the five hooks, but any host is a promise about the contract, not a directory of pre-written recipes. Today you'd write the Hetzner one yourself. The Rust kit's krunvm lane also can't deliver the kit's secrets yet — so if you stage them locally, it tells you to use docker or podman. And there is no fleet story. One deployment file is one machine. No regions array, no blue-green, no rolling orchestration. [sighs] We'd rather say that than imply a control plane that isn't there. And finally — two CLI dialects, in transition. The properties drawer with engine place — taught here, used by the shipped examples — and an older keyword form the Rust templates still emit. Learn the drawer form. It's the canon. Treat the other as drift to be normalized… not a second thing to learn.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need Docker? On a mac, no — local runs in a krunvm microVM, prereqs installed by doctor. The Rust kit also speaks docker and podman if you'd rather. Is local really identical to cloud? It's the same OCI image, booted from the same env-assembly function. What differs is the isolation mechanism and the axes you chose — not the engine. Can I add AWS, Hetzner, or Render? Yes — drop a directory with a bootstrap script that fills the five hooks. About ninety lines with different commands. The core never changes. Where do my secrets actually end up? Never in the file or the image. Values live in your environment or a locked-down secrets file, get forwarded into the recipe, staged through the provider, and land in the container's environment. Where does my data live locally, and does down delete it? It lives in a host directory bind-mounted to slash-data. And down preserves both your data and the APFS volume — it says so when it finishes. And — what if I just edit the deployment file by hand? [chuckles] That's the intended interface. Edit, validate, apply. And apply is idempotent — re-running on an unchanged file is a no-op. The file is the source; the verbs make reality match it.

tracks.title: Back up to nexus
tracks.text: So that's deployments. An org file of five properties the engine converges to — the place it runs being one of them. Inert by construction, read by a parser you could screenshot. The validator that refuses to let you lie. A microVM on your desk and a provider recipe in the cloud, both converging to the same image. [curious] This page was the how. The way back up is the why. Nexus — lesson 02 — for why you own an engine at all, and why local and cloud are a position, not a kind. Two formats stand beside this one — org, the format that stays inert here. And wbx, the command line that carries every verb. Everything the deployment does… is built from those.
